newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Tarmac boosts profit after shake-up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tarmac boosts profit after shake-up.

text.p: British building group Tarmac Plc cemented its recent restructuring with news on Tuesday of a rise in underlying pretax profits and an upbeat outlook for 1997 and beyond.
The better-than-expected figures and outlook bumped its shares up by eight pence to 112 by 1000 GMT.
Pretax profits for 1996 were 75.5 million pounds ($122.8 million) versus 67.1 million before accounting for a one-off charge of 65 million.
Analysts had been expecting profits before exceptional items at between 46.5 and 68 million pounds.
"The figures were very good, at the top end of expectations," said one share dealer.
Group saels grew to 2.66 billion from 2.48 billion and the final dividend payout was frozen at 5.5 pence per share.
Neville Simms, chief executive, said trading looked promising.
"The outlook for 1997 and beyond is much improved," he said in an interview.

"The year has started well in our UK markets. Across the group we are beginning to enjoy the benefits of additional growth opportunities and (the) stronger foundation created in 1996 at home and overseas."
Simms said that British gains would be made thanks to private sector growth in commercial building and millennium celebration and private finance initiative (PFI) projects.
"Government spending will remain subdued even if we do have a new administration," he said referring to the election set for May 1.
"But commercial building is up strongly and housing, the Millennium and PFI should all help fill the gap."
But on North American markets, he was more cautious. "I do anticipate a degree of slowing down. I'm not sure when," he said, adding it would be a "flattening rather than a dip".
The threat of interest rate rises in the United States and Britain could also take the edge off housing markets.
On the British election and a possible change of government after 18 years of Conservative rule, Tarmac expected a "neutral to mildly positive" outcome if the opposition Labour Party won power.
Simms said he also believed PFI would remain a policy priority for whoever formed the next government, once an "election hiatus" was over.

Turning to the results, the one-off charge of 65 million pounds related to Tarmac's integration of the former George Wimpey Plc minerals and construction businesses which were acquired in an asset swap for Tarmac's housing unit.
Simms said the cost savings from its restructuring had yielded 38 million -- double the original estimate.
He said the commercial benefits were still to be reaped. The asset swap leaves the group with two distinct businesseses -- heavy building materials and construction services.
Looking at a divisional breakdown, building materials saw total sales rise to 1.12 billion pounds from 930 million in 1995, with profits up sharply to 118.4 million from 92.9 million.
It showed growth in British and North American markets but fell back in other regions, including continental Europe.

Construction services sales grew to 1.51 billion from 1.01 billion, with profits of 15.9 million against 12.2 million. Again British markets moved ahead, with profits from the continent and elsewhere falling. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
